tier_reason: Peer-reviewed NSDI'14 paper compares mTCP against the stock Linux 3.10.12 TCP stack (BSD sockets + epoll, with and without SO_REUSEPORT) and MegaPipe; it names the CPU (Intel Xeon E5-2690 @ 2.90 GHz) and the benchmark apps are public in the repo (apps/example/epserver.c, epwget.c, apps/apache_benchmark, apps/lighttpd-1.4.32), but no compiler or flags are given, so it is not A.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Abstract: small-message transactions 25x faster than the latest Linux TCP stack and 3x faster than MegaPipe (best prior research system); popular applications 33% to 320% faster than on Linux. Sec 5.1: at 8 cores the 64B-message benchmark is 25x vs Linux 3.10.12 without SO_REUSEPORT, 5x vs Linux with SO_REUSEPORT, and 3x vs MegaPipe; connection accept is 13x/7.5x/5x vs Linux/REUSEPORT/multiprocess. lighttpd (SpecWeb2009 static files) is 3.2x/2.2x/1.5x vs Linux/REUSEPORT/MegaPipe; the SSLShader proxy is +18% to +33%.
corrections.hardware: Server: 1x 8-core Intel Xeon E5-2690 @ 2.90 GHz, 32 GB RAM, Intel 82599 10 GbE NIC; mTCP on Linux 2.6.32 (PSIO), baseline Linux 3.10.12 (ixgbe-3.17.3), MegaPipe on Linux 3.1.3
corrections.caveats: NSDI 2014 peer-reviewed paper; the CPU is stated but the compiler and flags are not, so the tier is B. The headline 25x is against Linux WITHOUT SO_REUSEPORT (a shared accept queue); against Linux with SO_REUSEPORT the gain is 5x at 8 cores. The baseline apps use the kernel's BSD sockets + epoll (the paper's Fig. 2 shows accept()/epoll_wait() vs mtcp_accept()/mtcp_epoll_wait()). The 2014 results used the PSIO driver on Linux 2.6.32. The core is BSD-3-Clause (GitHub reports NOASSERTION because of the template '<organization>' placeholder), but io_engine/ (PSIO driver) is GPL-2.0 and the dpdk submodule has its own licenses. There have been no commits on master since 2019-11.

notes: Numbers are verified in the paper's abstract, intro and Sec 5; I clarified that the 25x is against the non-SO_REUSEPORT configuration. The license was confirmed from the LICENSE text (Modified BSD); 2138 stars, not archived, not a fork, last commit 2019-11-18.

tier_reason: Upgraded from C to B. The OSDI'14 paper (peer-reviewed, Best Paper) measures Arrakis against a tuned Linux 3.8 kernel I/O path, including epoll (Table 2 breaks out epoll/recv/send/fsync costs, and haproxy is compared against Linux with and without SEPOLL). Public code does exist (github.com/UWNetworksLab/arrakis, MIT, with usr/bench/udp_echo), so the no-code cap no longer applies. It is not A: the paper gives no compiler or flags, and the ported Redis, memcached and haproxy builds are not in the public tree.

corrections.is_fork_of: http://www.barrelfish.org/ (README_ARRAKIS: 'a fork of Barrelfish release 2014-03-11'; not a GitHub fork)
corrections.baseline: epoll / Linux kernel I/O stack (Linux 3.8, Ubuntu 13.04, tuned ixgbe 3.17.3: sockets + epoll network path and VFS write/fsync storage path)
corrections.workload: Redis 2.8.5 persistent NoSQL store (GET/SET, 1 KB values, 65,536 keys, every SET persisted individually, 1,600 connections, single core), Arrakis/P (POSIX) vs Linux; also a UDP echo server, memcached 1.4.15 (90/10 get/set), haproxy 1.4.24 HTTP load balancing, and a raw-IP load-balancing middlebox.
corrections.claimed_speedup: Abstract: 2-5x lower latency and 9x higher throughput for Redis relative to a well-tuned Linux implementation (2x read latency, 5x write latency, 9x write throughput). Table 2: Redis read-hit latency 8.67 us Linux vs 4.07 us Arrakis/P, durable write 163.14 us vs 31.51 us (about 2.1x and 5.2x, derived from page data). Other results: UDP echo 2.3x (Arrakis/P) and 3.9x (Arrakis/N); memcached 1.7x on one core; haproxy 2.2x vs Linux and 2x vs Linux with SEPOLL (speculative epoll) on one core; IP middlebox 2.6x.
corrections.hardware: Six-machine cluster: 6-core Intel Xeon E5-2430 (Sandy Bridge) @ 2.2 GHz, Intel X520 (82599) 10 GbE, Intel MegaRAID RS3DC040 with 1 GB flash-backed DRAM in front of a 100 GB Intel DC S3700 SSD, Dell PowerConnect 8024F 10 GbE switch
corrections.caveats: Research OS (a Barrelfish fork) that needs SR-IOV NICs and IOMMU hardware; it is not a drop-in library. Much of the Redis write win comes from the storage path (fsync 137.84 us vs 24.26 us) and the custom Caladan/TenaciousD log, not just from bypassing epoll. Porting Caladan to Linux alone gave 5x write throughput. Sec 4.4 says 'write latency improves by 63%', which is inconsistent with the abstract's 5x taken from Table 2. The paper says Linux used offloads Arrakis lacked (TSO/LRO/DCA), so the comparison is weighted toward Linux. The public repo (MIT) contains the OS, the Arranet stack, TenaciousD and the UDP echo benchmark, but not the ported Redis, memcached or haproxy. The project site says Arrakis has been merged back into Barrelfish and is no longer maintained separately. No compiler or flags are given.

notes: Code does exist: arrakis.cs.washington.edu/download points to github.com/UWNetworksLab/arrakis (MIT, 267 stars, not archived, not a GitHub fork, last master commit 2014-05-22). The orchestrator should set repo_url to that URL (repo_url is not a correctable field here) and may re-key the id. All abstract numbers were verified in the paper PDF; the workload is real Redis 2.8.5, not 'Redis-like'.

tier_reason: First-party arXiv preprint (Oracle engineers, 'submitted to PVLDB', not yet peer-reviewed) comparing io_uring against the libaio path inside closed-source Oracle Database 26ai. The end-to-end numbers (Table 9-12) cannot be reproduced. The public artifact (github.com/rch0wdhury/iouring-rdbms-vldb-artifact; gcc -O2 Makefile) covers only the Sec 3 microbenchmarks and gives no CPU model for them, so neither A nor B applies.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Abstract and Table 9 (Oracle Database 26ai, 96 vCPUs, io_uring vs libaio baseline). Update IOPS (isolated DBWR write path): 1.067M to 1.428M write IOPS (+34%), CPU per physical write 58 to 41 us (-29%). Scan (150 GB, direct-path reads): CPU per read -19% at unchanged throughput. TPC-C: tpmC unchanged (2.275M vs 2.279M); server CPU 45.0% to 43.8% (-1.2 pp) only after cutting DBWR processes from 32 to 23; with the same 32 DBWR it was 45.7%. TPC-H: CPU per query -8.5% geometric mean, elapsed time within noise. Async I/O submit wait is about 75x lower. Synchronous single-block reads stay on pread (io_uring shows no gain there, and CPU/IO is about 2x higher at 512 KB-1 MB). Microbenchmark (Fig 3): geometric mean -39% CPU per I/O vs batched libaio, up to +15% IOPS in CPU-bound regimes.
corrections.hardware: End-to-end: OCI BM.DenseIO.E4 bare metal, AMD EPYC 7J13 (128 cores, 96 vCPUs given to the DB), 2 TB RAM, 8 local NVMe SSDs in software RAID-0, Oracle Linux with UEK R8. Microbenchmarks: a single NVMe device; the CPU is not stated separately.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: Microbenchmark artifact only: gcc -O2 -Wall -Wextra -pthread (Makefile, compiler version not stated). Build flags for the Oracle Database 26ai internal build are not stated.
corrections.workload: Oracle Database 26ai (internal development build): a synthetic Update IOPS test (DBWR write-flush path), a 150 GB parallel direct-path Scan, TPC-C (5K warehouses, 210 users) and the 22-query TPC-H (1.1 TB, uncalibrated/unaudited), plus Sec 3 microbenchmarks (libaio vs six io_uring configurations on a single NVMe, block-size x device-count sweep). io_uring replaces libaio on the async batched paths; synchronous reads stay on pread.
corrections.caveats: First-party benchmark by Oracle engineers of their own closed-source product; arXiv preprint submitted to PVLDB, not yet peer-reviewed. The TPC-C/TPC-H runs are unaudited and 'for internal comparison only'. Gains are almost entirely CPU efficiency, not latency or elapsed time: the TPC-C 1.2 pp CPU saving needs DBWR cut from 32 to 23, and TPC-H elapsed times are unchanged. The mechanism is the Linux io_uring interface through a custom thin layer that does not use liburing, so this is effectively io_uring-vs-libaio evidence rather than a reusable library. Artifact: github.com/rch0wdhury/iouring-rdbms-vldb-artifact (Zenodo 10.5281/zenodo.20099105, CC-BY-4.0 on Zenodo, no LICENSE file on GitHub, 1 star) holds only the microbenchmarks. The shared buffer registration work led to IORING_REGISTER_CLONE_BUFFERS in Linux 6.12.

notes: All record numbers match the abstract and Tables 9-12. The 'synchronous reads' regression is against pread, not libaio. The orchestrator may prefer to file this as is_evidence_for_known for io_uring (https://github.com/axboe/liburing is in known_seed) rather than as a standalone entry, since the Oracle code is proprietary; I kept has_code=false because the only public code is the microbenchmark artifact.
